newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cavallo links Mercosur success to foreign capital.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo links Mercosur success to foreign capital.

text.p: Former Argentine economy minister Domingo Cavallo urged South American leaders to further unshackle their economies to lure foreign investment and strengthen the region's four-nation Mercosur customs union.

"It's important that political figures send the right signals (to foreign investors) and remove the obstacles that restrict competitiveness and growth," Cavallo told a seminar on Mercosur's participation in world markets.

The controversial former minister -- a permanent fixture of the Latin American lecture circuit since resigning in July -- said foreign investment was crucial to the ongoing success of Mercosur because domestic savings in the four countries were not sufficient to finance economic growth.

Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay formed Mercosur in 1995 after years of talks. Mercosur members consider the customs union an enormous success, noting that trade among its partners grew to $15 billion a year in 1995 from $4 billion in 1990.
Exports from non-Mercosur countries entering the customs union totalled $55 billion in 1995, up from $25 billion in 1990.

But Mercosur has come under some criticism, notably from the World Bank, which said the union has helped trade and investment among its members but mostly benefits sectors unable to compete in world markets, like the auto industry.

Cavallo said removing restrictive labor laws, tax codes and other bureaucratic limitations to growth and investment was among the biggest challenges facing Mercosur leaders. He said that such deregulation had to be carried out to avoid creating a closed, uncompetitive trade bloc.
Cavallo was joined by other speakers who highlighted the need for strong foreign participation to develop Merscosur.
Winston Fritsch, president of Banco Kleinwort Benson Brasil, said Mercosur's most important investments over the next decade were in telecommunications, the power sector, schools and roads.
"Just in Brazil, the World Bank estimates that $1 billion in infrastructure investment is needed each week," Fritsch said.

Foreign investment has and will continue to play an important role in the privatization of state-owned telephone and power firms in the region, Fritsch said. He added that foreign firms were also playing a key role in making the private sector more competitive.

"Eight out of 10 mergers and acquisitions in Brazil have had the participation of foreign investors," he said, noting that many Brazilian firms have gone out of business or been bought out by competitors following economic opening.

He said that economic stabilization, in the form of low inflation and steady currencies, has given foreign firms the confidence to make sizeable investments in Mercosur countries over the past few years.
But he and Cavallo warned that the region's governments had to stick to tough stabilization plans in order to cement the conditions that will attract steady long-term foreign investment.
